name: Home Assistant Cloud
subcategory: family organization, recipes and household inventory
tagline: Self-host smart-home control and use a user-owned remote-access tunnel

tiers.name: Home Assistant Cloud
tiers.limits: Remote access, text-to-speech APIs, voice assistants/integrations and support for Home Assistant/Open Home development.
tiers.notes: $65/year in USA/International; local taxes excluded where applicable.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free Home Assistant Cloud tier; Home Assistant itself can be self-hosted locally without Nabu Casa Cloud.
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; Stripe/credit cards/Google Pay/Apple Pay and PayPal supported
pricing.hiddenCosts: Regional prices differ: US/International $6.50/mo or $65/yr; EU €7.50/mo or €75/yr VAT included; UK £6.50/mo or £65/yr VAT included; Canada CAD 8.70/mo or CAD 87/yr.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Home Assistant Cloud, self-host smart-home control and use a user-owned remote-access tunnel. The hard boundary is managed remote access, voice integrations, funding for open source, and low-maintenance security, plus sync, integrations, and household adoption.
coreLoopDIY: Self-host smart-home control, reach it remotely through a user-owned tunnel, and keep automation data portable and owner-controlled.
whatYouLose: managed remote access, voice integrations, funding for open source, and low-maintenance security
ongoingBurden: multi-user conflicts, reminders, notifications, imports, barcode data, smart-home APIs, backups, and long-term maintenance
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Home Assistant Cloud because household apps survive when every family member actually uses them and the data stays current across devices. The recurring cost buys multi-user conflicts, reminders, notifications, imports, barcode data, smart-home APIs, backups, and long-term maintenance, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Mealie
priorArt.desc: Active open-source recipe manager and meal planner for households.

alternatives.name: AmneziaVPN
alternatives.desc: Point it at your VPS and it builds a private route home; remote access is yours, voice integrations are not.

facts.install: Install the desktop/mobile client, then give it root SSH access to a compatible Linux VPS so it can deploy the server
facts.dataFormat: Private keys and connection profiles are held by the Amnezia clients; protocol containers and server configuration live on the user-controlled VPS, and tunneled traffic exits through that server rather than an Amnezia-operated VPN fleet.
facts.gapVsPaid: Amnezia restores private remote access only; it does not provide Home Assistant Cloud's Alexa and Google Assistant bridging, webhooks, text-to-speech endpoints, managed certificates, or support.
facts.setupBlocker: The unavoidable first obstacle is obtaining and paying for a public VPS, then handing the app root SSH credentials and keeping that server patched and reachable.

alternatives.name: NetBird
alternatives.desc: A free managed private network to your Home Assistant, with routes and access rules instead of port forwarding.

facts.install: Hosted signup plus a client on each device, or the official Docker-based self-hosting quickstart
facts.dataFormat: WireGuard keys are generated and kept on peers; device inventory, users, routes, groups, and access policies live in NetBird Cloud or the self-hosted management database, while payload traffic normally travels peer-to-peer and may traverse NetBird relay infrastructure when direct connectivity fails.
facts.gapVsPaid: NetBird gives enrolled devices a private route home, but guests, webhooks, and voice assistants cannot use it like a public Nabu Casa endpoint and the user must manage network policy.
facts.setupBlocker: The managed free service installs cleanly; self-hosting adds a public domain, TLS, identity/authentication, open ports, relay configuration, a management database, and upgrades.

alternatives.name: Tailscale Personal
alternatives.desc: Remote Home Assistant access without port forwarding; voice-assistant bridging and vendor support stay paid.

facts.install: Install Tailscale on each device and sign them into the same free Personal tailnet
facts.dataFormat: WireGuard private keys stay on enrolled devices; device identity, public keys, ACLs, routes, and coordination metadata live in Tailscale's control plane, while encrypted payload traffic is peer-to-peer when possible and otherwise crosses DERP relays.
facts.gapVsPaid: Tailscale makes private remote access easy, but every client must join the tailnet and it does not replace Nabu Casa's public URL, voice-assistant linking, cloud webhooks, or Home Assistant support.

alternatives.name: wg-easy
alternatives.desc: A self-hosted WireGuard doorway to Home Assistant; certificates, DNS, and uptime remain your hobbies.

facts.install: Docker Compose on a Linux host with a public UDP port
facts.dataFormat: WireGuard server configuration, peer records, private keys, and generated client profiles live in the mounted `/etc/wireguard` data volume on the host; tunneled traffic exits through that host.
facts.gapVsPaid: wg-easy provides only a WireGuard doorway, leaving server uptime, port forwarding, DNS, certificates, client setup, voice-assistant bridging, webhooks, and troubleshooting to the household.
facts.setupBlocker: A non-expert still needs a Linux server or home port-forward, Docker, a WireGuard-capable kernel, UDP 51820 reachability, privileged network capabilities, DNS, and safe web-admin exposure.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Cloud plan and a single-household organizer DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Home Assistant Cloud in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, SQLite, Drizzle ORM, and a local-first PWA; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: self-host smart-home control, reach it remotely through a user-owned tunnel, and keep automation data portable and owner-controlled.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create household members, shared lists, calendar items, recipes or inventory records, and assignments.
Provide fast mobile-first capture with large controls, offline queueing, and conflict-safe sync to one server.
Support recurring chores or events, reminders, completion history, and printable views.
Add CSV or JSON import and export plus photo attachments with clear size limits.
Allow private and shared items and make every change attributable and undoable.
Add backups, household export, member removal, and a simple invite code.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out retailer ordering and proprietary product catalogs.
Deliberately leave out broad smart-home integrations.
Deliberately leave out large public recipe libraries and polished native mobile clients.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
